summary: Measurements are noisy and you usually have more of them than unknowns. You derive the normal equations by setting a gradient to zero, fit a motor’s torque constant from bench data, and check the fit recovers the true value within 1 % at a 20 dB signal-to-noise ratio.
html:
More equations than unknowns

You want a motor’s torque constant kt​ in τ=kt​i. You measure torque at many currents. Each measurement gives one equation, and with noise no single kt​ satisfies them all. Stack them as Ax≈b with more rows than columns and look for the x that makes the residual r=Ax−b as small as possible in the squared sense:

xmin​ J(x)=∥Ax−b∥2=(Ax−b)⊤(Ax−b).

The normal equations

Expand J=x⊤A⊤Ax−2b⊤Ax+b⊤b. Its gradient is

∇J=2A⊤Ax−2A⊤b.

Setting it to zero gives the normal equations

A⊤Ax=A⊤b.

Geometrically, A⊤(Ax−b)=0 says the residual is perpendicular to every column of A: the best fit is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space. The matrix A⊤A is square, symmetric and invertible when the columns of A are independent.

For a line through the origin, A is the single column of currents and the formula reduces to

kt​=∑j​ij2​∑j​ij​τj​​.

Worked example: four bench points

Current i [A] 1 2 3 4
Torque τ [N·m] 0.08 0.15 0.23 0.30

Through the origin. ∑iτ=0.08+0.30+0.69+1.20=2.27 and ∑i2=30, so kt​=2.27/30=0.07567 N·m/A.

With an offset τ=kt​i+c, the columns are i and a column of ones:

A⊤A=(3010​104​),A⊤b=(2.270.76​)⇒kt​=0.0740, c=0.005.

The small positive offset is friction torque the motor must overcome before the output moves. Ignoring it biases kt​ upward by about 2 %.

Code it from scratch

This fits kt​ and c by forming the normal equations and solving them with your own elimination code, then checks the 1 % target at 20 dB SNR using 5000 samples, a five-second log at 1 kHz. With only 200 samples the standard error of kt​ is about 1.5 %, so the target would fail about half the time.

fit_kt.py
import numpy as np

def solve(M, v):                       # small Gaussian elimination with pivoting
    M = np.array(M, float); v = np.array(v, float); n = len(v)
    for k in range(n):
        p = k + np.argmax(abs(M[k:, k])); M[[k, p]] = M[[p, k]]; v[[k, p]] = v[[p, k]]
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            l = M[i, k] / M[k, k]; M[i] -= l * M[k]; v[i] -= l * v[k]
    x = np.zeros(n)
    for i in reversed(range(n)):
        x[i] = (v[i] - M[i, i + 1:] @ x[i + 1:]) / M[i, i]
    return x

def lstsq_normal(A, b):
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    return solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ b)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    i = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4.]); tau = np.array([0.08, 0.15, 0.23, 0.30])
    k0 = lstsq_normal(i[:, None], tau)[0]
    k1, c1 = lstsq_normal(np.column_stack([i, np.ones(4)]), tau)
    assert abs(k0 - 0.075667) < 1e-6 and abs(k1 - 0.074) < 1e-9 and abs(c1 - 0.005) < 1e-9

    rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
    kt, c = 0.075, 0.01
    cur = rng.uniform(0.5, 10, 5000)          # a 5 s log at 1 kHz
    clean = kt * cur + c
    sigma = np.sqrt(np.mean(clean ** 2)) / 10      # 20 dB: noise rms is a tenth of signal rms
    meas = clean + rng.normal(0, sigma, cur.size)
    k_hat, c_hat = lstsq_normal(np.column_stack([cur, np.ones_like(cur)]), meas)
    err = abs(k_hat - kt) / kt
    print(f"k_t = {k_hat:.5f} N·m/A (error {100*err:.2f} %), offset {c_hat:.4f} N·m")
    assert err < 0.01

Forming A⊤A squares the condition number of the problem (lesson 13). For a two-parameter motor fit that is harmless; for high-order polynomial fits it loses accuracy, and the QR method of the next lesson avoids it.

Exercises

Fit y=mx to the points (1,2.1), (2,3.9), (3,6.2).

Show the solution
  1. ∑xy=2.1+7.8+18.6=28.5, ∑x2=14.
  2. m=28.5/14=2.0357.

Show that the least-squares residual of a fit with an offset column sums to zero.

Show the solution
  1. The normal equations say A⊤r=0, so r is perpendicular to every column.
  2. One column is all ones, so 1⊤r=∑j​rj​=0. A fitted line with an intercept always passes through the mean of the data.

Quiz

quiz.q: Fit τ=kt​i (no offset) to the four bench points. What is kt​ in N·m/A?
quiz.explain: 2.27/30=0.07567.

quiz.q: Fit y=mx to (1,2.1), (2,3.9), (3,6.2). What is m?
quiz.explain: 28.5/14=2.0357.

quiz.q: What does the equation A⊤(Ax−b)=0 say geometrically?
quiz.explain: Each row of A⊤ is a column of A, and its dot product with the residual is zero.
options: The residual is perpendicular to every column of A

quiz.q: A 20 dB signal-to-noise ratio means the signal power is how many times the noise power?
quiz.explain: 1020/10=100, so the noise rms is a tenth of the signal rms.

quiz.q: Why can forming A⊤A be a bad idea for ill-conditioned problems?
quiz.explain: κ(A⊤A)=κ(A)2, so a problem with κ=107 becomes one with 1014.
options: It squares the condition number, amplifying round-off
It needs more memory than A
